title: urnetwork / extenders
description: The extender network: population and reachability, what is published in dns, the gossip release queue, which extenders carry the contract load, the pings providers and extenders measure of each other, with how targets answer them (connect/GEOMAP.md §2.7), and the locations derived from those pings (§5.4), with what deriving them costs against the solve's budget (§5.3). Fed by the stats collector (controller/stats_collector.go) and the dns publish tick (taskworker/work/extender_dns_metrics.go).

panels.title: online extenders
panels.description: Active extenders with at least one active address — the population the drip rotates through and the directory publishes. Series are per process and keyed by instance, so this aggregates across the fleet rather than selecting a bare series: during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: ipv4 only
panels.description: Online extenders reachable only over ipv4.

panels.title: ipv6 only
panels.description: Online extenders reachable only over ipv6. The scarce family: the gossip sampler and the dns sets both target an even split, so a small number here is what makes the fallback visible.

panels.title: dual stack
panels.description: Online extenders reachable over both families. These satisfy either side of the sampler's interleave and are the most useful members of the population.

panels.title: countries
panels.description: Distinct countries with at least one online extender.

panels.title: contracts with an extender (24h)
panels.description: Transfer contracts created in the last 24 hours with at least one extender party.

panels.title: population by ip family
panels.description: How the population splits by reachability. Both samplers aim for an even number of v4- and v6-reachable extenders and fall back to whatever exists, so a persistent gap here is what limits a v6-only client's choice.

panels.title: online extenders
panels.description: The population over time. A step down without a matching revocation release usually means addresses aged out of probing rather than extenders leaving.

panels.title: addresses in dns (v4)
panels.description: IPv4 addresses the last publish tick wrote across every A set. Series are per process and keyed by instance, so this aggregates across the fleet rather than selecting a bare series: during a redeploy the draining and starting processes both push.

panels.title: addresses in dns (v6)
panels.description: IPv6 addresses the last publish tick wrote across every AAAA set.

panels.title: extenders in dns
panels.description: Distinct extenders reachable through the addresses the last tick published. Lower than the population: each set is a rotating sample, not the whole pool.

panels.title: signed TXT records
panels.description: Signed extender records published across all TXT sets. Zero means the operator has no root key and only address sets were written — a client can then bootstrap addresses but cannot verify them.

panels.title: A sets
panels.description: A record sets published — one per continent with ipv4 addresses, plus the global default.

panels.title: AAAA sets
panels.description: AAAA record sets published. A family with no address anywhere produces no set at all rather than an empty one, since a record that resolves to nothing is worse than no record.

panels.title: addresses published by family
panels.description: What each tick actually wrote. The sets are recomputed every tick and never stored, so these gauges are the only record of what is in dns — the database can only say what was eligible.

panels.title: record sets by type
panels.description: Sets published per tick by record type. TXT tracks the locations the address sets answer for, so it should move with A and AAAA; TXT falling to zero alone means signing stopped.

panels.title: pending records
panels.description: Extender records written but not yet released to the gossip network. Should sit near zero; a count that does not fall means releases are not reaching the network while activations keep writing.

panels.title: pending revocations
panels.description: Revocations written but not yet released. These matter more than records: until one lands, clients keep trusting a withdrawn extender.

panels.title: oldest pending
panels.description: Age of the oldest unreleased message of any kind. Climbing steadily is the clearest sign the publisher is stuck — the pending count alone can look healthy while one message sits forever.

panels.title: records released (24h)
panels.description: Extender records released to the gossip network in the last 24 hours, including the drip re-releasing the same extender.

panels.title: revocations released (24h)
panels.description: Revocations released in the last 24 hours.

panels.title: extenders released (24h)
panels.description: Distinct extenders behind those record releases. Much lower than the release count means the drip is re-announcing a few extenders rather than the network learning new ones.

panels.title: release queue depth
panels.description: The gossip release backlog. Rows are written by activation, by a probe that loses an extender's last address, and by the drip; they are drained by the gossip publisher.

panels.title: oldest pending message
panels.description: Age of the oldest unreleased message per kind. A sawtooth is normal — it resets each time the queue drains. A ramp that never resets is a stuck publisher.

panels.title: released to the network (24h)
panels.description: What the network learned over the trailing 24 hours. The gap between records and distinct extenders is drip re-announcement.

panels.title: busiest extenders
panels.description: Contracts carried per extender over the dashboard's time range, most first, top 20. Derived from a single per-extender counter accumulated from closed hour buckets, so the same metric answers any range without a new gauge; widen the time picker to rank over a week. sum by extender_id merges a redeploy's overlapping processes, and increase() handles the counter reset a restart causes.

panels.title: contract load per extender
panels.description: Contracts per hour for the twenty busiest extenders, as a time series. This is the view the leaderboard cannot give: whether load is concentrated on a few extenders or spread, and whether that changes over the day. Each line is one extender; a fleet where everyone carries a similar load and one where three carry everything are visibly different here.

panels.title: pings (24h)
panels.description: Every ping the operator stored in the last 24 hours (connect/GEOMAP.md §2.5): a provider or an extender measured its round trip to an extender and reported it itself, over its own credential, with whatever the target answered. Every verdict counts and so does a ping relayed through an NLayer chain; the panels beside this one say which. A consumer client probes to rank without identifying itself, so this never counts consumers.

panels.title: co-signed (24h)
panels.description: Pings whose target co-signed them, as the operator recomputed it: the target's co-signature verified under the target's stored key over exactly the claim the pinger signed. Only these are measurements (D8). Well below the total means targets are refusing or not answering; the refusals table below says which.

panels.title: refused (24h)
panels.description: Pings the pinger says its target refused, plus acceptances whose co-signature did not verify. A refusal is the pinger's word only and is evidence against a target only in aggregate (GEOMAP §5.5); a ping that got no verdict at all is counted apart as unknown, so a flaky path is not read as a refusing extender.

panels.title: providers measuring (24h)
panels.description: Distinct providers with a ping stored in the window. A provider probes on start and on its 12 hour refresh, so this is roughly the providers that ran in the window; well below the online provider count means most providers are not reaching extenders, or not reporting what they measured.

panels.title: extenders measuring (24h)
panels.description: Distinct extenders with a ping of another extender stored in the window (GEOMAP §2.1). Every extender pings every peer in its directory within a day, so this should track the online extender count; a gap is extenders on a binary without the peer pinger, or reporters that cannot reach the operator.

panels.title: extenders pinged (24h)
panels.description: Distinct extenders that were the target of at least one stored ping in the window. Compare with the online extender count: an extender that is online but never pinged is unreachable from every pinger, or absent from their directories.

panels.title: pings by kind and outcome (24h)
panels.description: The trailing 24 hour ping count over time, split by who pinged (provider or extender), what the operator made of the target's verdict (cosigned, rejected, unknown) and whether the ping was relayed. A relayed ping (GEOMAP §2.9) went through an NLayer extender, which relays a probe to the end of its chain: the round trip is the whole chain's, the claim is judged and co-signed by the chain end, and the row counts here and as co-signature evidence but is never a solver term, since the detour through the front overstates the distance to the end. Every series is published, zero included, so a verdict that goes quiet is a line at zero rather than a gap.

panels.title: extender↔extender pings per hour
panels.description: Pings stored per hour by pinger kind, from the per-extender counter: extenders pinging each other, the edges between the nodes with the most stable positions (GEOMAP §2), beside providers pinging extenders. An extender with P peers pings about 2P times a day, so the extender series should grow with the square of the fleet. The counter is fed from closed hour buckets, so the last hour is always a step behind; a flat zero with extenders online means the peer pinger or its reporter is down, not that nobody measured.

panels.title: most pinged extenders
panels.description: Pings per target extender over the dashboard's time range, every pinger kind and verdict, most first, top 20. The counter is the same shape as the contracts counter: one series per extender and pinger kind fed from closed hour buckets, capped with topk so an open population never renders one line per extender, read through increase() so a restart's counter reset does not show as a drop. sum by extender_id merges the pinger kinds and a redeploy's overlapping processes.

panels.title: pings per extender
panels.description: Pings per hour for the twenty most pinged extenders. Capped with topk for the same reason as the table -- the extender population is open -- and read through increase() because it is a counter. Whether pings concentrate on a few extenders or spread across the fleet is what this shows; the continent hint, the latency ordering and the peer pinger should spread them.

panels.title: targets refusing the most
panels.description: The share of each target's pings that were refused over the dashboard's time range, highest first, top 20, among targets with at least ten pings in the range so one refused ping is not a 100% row. This is the evidence the co-signature exists for (GEOMAP §2.3, §2.7): an extender that never co-signs, or refuses far more than its peers, is one rejecting valid readings -- or one many pingers lie about, which is why a refusal is only the pinger's word and is weighed in aggregate by the reputation of §5.5. A ping with no verdict is not a refusal and is not counted here. Both counters are per-extender, fed from closed hour buckets, capped with topk and read through increase().

panels.title: refusals per hour
panels.description: Refused pings stored per hour across the fleet, from the per-extender rejections counter. A step up that the ping rate does not share is a target, or a group of them, starting to refuse; the table beside this one names them. Fed from closed hour buckets, so the last hour is a step behind.

panels.title: derived locations
panels.description: Providers and extenders with a published derived location (connect/GEOMAP.md §5.4): nodes whose co-signed, direct pings placed them better than their genesis, with at least three pings to at least three peers. Every other node keeps its genesis, so this is expected to be well below the population. Counted from the table, which holds exactly what the last derivation published and loses a row a day after the derivation that wrote it (§5.7), so a node that stops pinging falls back to its genesis on its own and drops out of this count.

panels.title: crossed region
panels.description: Published derived locations whose mapped place (§6) lies outside the region their genesis placed them in; a country crossing counts here too. The containment terms of the solve (§5.2) price every crossing, so one that survives is the pings insisting, not an error. A handful is normal at region borders; a rising count is how a wrong genesis, a miscalibrated k, or a colluding cluster first shows (§5.4).

panels.title: crossed country
panels.description: Published derived locations whose mapped place lies outside the country their genesis placed them in. The country term is weighted far above the region term, since GeoLite2's country is far more reliable than its city (§5.2, D10), so this should be near zero; any is worth a look, and a jump is the strongest early sign of a colluding cluster or a bad genesis source. These nodes are published in the derived country: provider search and the extender record's country and continent follow it (§6).

panels.title: excluded sources (last run)
panels.description: Sources the last derivation left out of its solve on reputation (§5.5): past four sigma from the population on scatter, bias or a refusal rate. An excluded source's own measurements carry no weight; it is still placed from what others measured of it. Normal is zero or a few; the derive job's log names every one. Recorded by the derivation, so it holds its value between runs and across taskworker restarts.

panels.title: ping residual (last run)
panels.description: The RMS ping residual, d(p_s, p_t) − d̂_st, over the last derivation's final solve, in km, at the derived positions (§5.2, §5.4). The panel below sets it against the same residual at genesis, which the derivation exists to reduce. It moves with the population's spread of detours and queues; a drift with no change in the population is how a miscalibrated k or o shows.

panels.title: since the last derivation
panels.description: Time since the last derivation (§5.3, §5.7). The derive job runs every 8 hours, so this saw-tooths between zero and 8 h. Amber past 9 h, a run is late; red past 16 h, two were missed, and the published rows are expiring without being renewed, so nodes are falling back to genesis. No data means no derivation has been recorded yet, which is normal until the first run 8 hours after deploy.

panels.title: derived locations by kind
panels.description: Published derived locations over time, providers and extenders apart. Each derivation replaces the set whole, so steps land every 8 hours; between them the count only falls, as the hourly sweep removes rows a day old (§5.7). Both kinds are always published, zero included.

panels.title: crossings
panels.description: Published derived locations mapped outside their genesis region and country, over time (§5.4, §6). The country line should sit near zero; a region line that climbs while the population does not is the first sign of a wrong genesis source, a miscalibrated k, or a colluding cluster.

panels.title: excluded sources
panels.description: Sources each derivation left out on reputation (§5.5), as a step per run. Reputation is recomputed from the day's pings on every run and nothing accumulates, so a source that stops misbehaving leaves this count within a day.

panels.title: ping residual
panels.description: The RMS ping residual of each derivation's final solve, in km, at the derived positions and at genesis (§5.4). The derived line is expected to sit well below the genesis line; the gap is what the derivation adds over GeoLite2 alone. The two converging means the pings have stopped improving on genesis.

panels.title: projected solve time (share of budget)
panels.description: The planner's projection of the next derivation's solve time at the taskworker host's cores, as a share of MaxSolveSeconds (GEOMAP §5.3, "Scale"). Every run projects the next from its own measured seconds per term and per node sweep, the sweeps it took and a safety factor, so this moves with the fleet, one step a run. Amber from 80 %, where SIGNALS.md §2.19c raises its capacity finding (DeriveCapacityMargin); red at the budget. The job does not partition past it: the answer is more cores on the taskworker host.

panels.title: projected solve memory (share of budget)
panels.description: The planner's projection of the next derivation's peak heap, as a share of MaxSolveBytes (GEOMAP §5.3, "Scale"): the last run's measured bytes per term and per node at the next run's counts. The heap is sampled while the day is read and solved, and includes garbage not yet collected, so the projection errs high. Amber from 80 %, where SIGNALS.md §2.19c raises its capacity finding; red at the budget, past which the answer is more memory on the taskworker host.

panels.title: last solve
panels.description: The wall time of the last derivation's solve and mapping (GEOMAP §5.3): three reputation rounds of parallel Jacobi sweeps over every term, on the taskworker host's cores. Seconds at a few thousand nodes, a minute or two at the scale target; the projection beside it is this, scaled to the next run's counts and cores.

panels.title: last read of the day
panels.description: The wall time of the last derivation reading the day's co-signed pings over its concurrent cursors, one pinger-id hash range each, aggregating into terms as the rows arrive (GEOMAP §5.3, "Scale"). It grows with the rows, not the pairs; a jump with no change in the fleet is the database, not the job.

panels.title: solve time against its budget
panels.description: Each derivation's measured solve time, the planner's projection of the next at the taskworker host's cores, and MaxSolveSeconds, over time (GEOMAP §5.3, "Scale"). The projection runs about three times the measurement, the safety factor for a run that takes more sweeps than the last. A projection climbing toward the budget is the fleet outgrowing the host's cores; SIGNALS.md §2.19c finds it at 80 %.

panels.title: solve memory against its budget
panels.description: Each derivation's peak heap over its read of the day and its solve, the planner's projection of the next, and MaxSolveBytes, over time (GEOMAP §5.3, "Scale"). The aggregation keeps a bounded reservoir of samples per ordered pair, so the heap follows the pairs, not the pings. A projection climbing toward the budget is the fleet outgrowing the host's memory; SIGNALS.md §2.19c finds it at 80 %.
